factors.name: The name of the factor. If you just want to add a bunch all at once to brainstorm, you can just add the name and come back to the other stuff later.
factors.optimal: What do you want this factor to be? For instance, if taste is on a scale of 0-10, then we probably want it to taste good (10), but if it's cost, we probably don't want it to be expensive (0). If you just know you want it to be as high or low as possible (given the provided answers), you can select "Min" or "Max".
factors.weight: How much do you care about this factor? For instance, we probably don't care much about how many leftovers a meal has, but we probably care a more about what it tastes like. If you're unsure, the Fine Tune Weights page can help you set these, so you don't need to worry about it too much yet.
factors.scale: What are the bounds of this factor? For instance, if it's on a scale of 0-10, then we probably want it to be between 0 and 10. If it's not clear, however, you can select "Calculate" to automatically calculate it from the answers you give. There may also be one but not the other, for example, for the "cost" factor, we know it's not negative (no one is going to pay a *us* for a meal), but it could cost as much as we want. However, if you know you're not going to spend more than $100, you can set the max to 100. Adding a scale explicitly is going to be more accurate for a single value than leaving it unbounded. For comparing multiple values, it shouldn't matter.
factors.unit: This is to help you keep track of what the scale is, it's not used in the math of the decision at all. You can have the scale be anything you want, 0-10, dollars, miles, etc. For vauge factors, for example Taste or happiness, it's usually easiest to use a 0-10 scale. Note that you can use arbitrary labels for numbers, but they have to be on a continuous scale (for example, "0: small, 1: medium, 2: big" works, but "0: Idaho, 1: Tennessee, 2: Utah" doesn't)
factors.factor: The name of the factor. You can put anything here: from "taste", to "happiness" to "how much I want to". Literally anything you can think of that relates to the decision you're making. The more the better! Even things that are only slightly relevant will make the final answer more accurate.
factors.explanation:
This page allows you to add, edit, and remove factors to your decision. Add factors by filling out the fields and pressing "Add", or click on a factor in the table to modify it.

Factors are anything that relates to the decision. Anything that would go on a pro-con list would be a factor. You can add as many as you want, more factors the better, but idealy they should represent unique concepts (for example, `does the meal taste good` and `does the meal make me happy` might be a little too similar). Feel free to be as specific as you want.

Hover over each box for more details.

You can also add weights (how much you care) on the "Fine Tune Weights" page for a more convenient interface.

dashboard.explanation: This is where you add new decisions, or switch between what decision you're currently evaluating. They will be preserved in this browser, but you can also download and import them later for safe keeping. You can also load a couple of examples if you just want to mess with the site and see how it works. You can also import/export to a spreadsheet, as well as your Google Drive. Note that Google Drive integration is NOT automatic. Also, at the moment, if you want to use it, text Cope and he'll add you to the testing list (auth stuff)

weights.explanation:
This is where you can fine tune how much each factor matters. Because getting
the weights right can have a large impact on the final answer, I've created a
seperate way to break it down as well. Remember, this is targeted towards making
big decisions that might have lots of factors.

If you think the weights you added when adding factors are already pretty accurate,
you can skip this step.

There's steps to fine tuning the factors. You can do either one, both, or neither
of them as you'd like. First, you can go through the section that helps you sort
the factors in order of importance. It breaks it down into pairs of factors
and asks which is more important. It uses a custom algorithm to make the sorting
as efficient as possible. It won't change any of the weights until you're done
sorting them, and then it will ask you if you want to set them as the new weights.

From there, you can go to the slider, which shows the weights next to each other.
You can adjust the weights by dragging the sliders, so they're not simply evenly
spaced. I've also included several graphs to help you visualize the weights.

Once you're done here, head over to the `Answers` page to start making the
decision.

decisions.explanation:
This lets you look over your decision before viewing the results. You can edit cells directly by double clicking them, and add, remove, or rename factors and options if you need.

Once you're satisfied that it all looks good, you can move onto the Results page!

options.explanation:
This page allows you to add, remove, and rename options in your decision. If you don't have any options yet, you're just planning ahead, that's fine! You don't have to add anything yet.

Once you're done here, go to the `Factors` page to add factors to your decision.

quiz.explanation:
Now that you've specified what the decision you're trying to make actually is, you can start inputting what you know. This page breaks down the decision into parts so you can evaluate each part of the decision induvidually. This part usually takes the longest. If you're not sure about an answer, you can skip it and come back to it later, or you can select "I'm not sure" and provide a range of values that you think is appropriate. The behind the scenes algorithm will take your uncertainty into account.

There are 2 options for inputting answers: 

1.A quiz, which will ask you each answer one at a time, and you can input it interactively. 

2. A manual input table, in which you can put the answers in directly, if that makes more sense to you. 

Once you're finished filling in all the answers, you can move on to the `View Results` page to finally see the results of your decision!

results.explanation:
This page shows the results of your decision. It shows the best option, the worst option, and graphs of the results to help you understand why they're the best and worst.

When providing feedback, you can use the letters on the right side to reference specific graphs.
results.line1d: This shows the results in terms of how "bad" each option is, or in other words, how far way each option is from the optimal. This doesn't mean any given option is a "bad option", bad in this sense just means "less good"
results.PCA: This shows each option as a point in 2D space. Each point is actually in a much higher dimension, but this is projected down to 2D to make it easier to visualize. (For those who are interested, it uses the PCA algorithm to do this.)
results.radar: Here you can compare options directly. The more area that overlaps with the Theoretical Best option, the better it is. The more area that overlaps with the Theoretical Worst option, the worse it is. You can click and drag the edge of the graph to rotate it, so you can see all the factors.
results.heatmap1d: This shows your options in order of how good they are. The greener, the better. If all of the options are green, that means all of them are generally good options. If they're all red, that means you don't have many good options. The percentage is on a scale of worst possible to best possible.
results.entropy: This shows how much each factor contributed to the decision. The height of the bar corresponds to the "variability" of each factor, and the width corresponds to the weight you assigned to that factor, so you can think of the area as the "usefulness" of the factor. For example, say you have a factor that we care a lot about, but which you gave similar answers for on each option. That factor didn't really contribute much to the decision, because they're all about the same. But if all of the options are different for a given factor, then that's going to be a more useful factor. However, if we don't care about that factor, it still won't matter much. NOTE: if you're looking at this graph and going "Really? That doesn't seem right...", you probably need to go back and adjust your weights.
results.goodness_bar: This shows how good each option is on a scale of worst possible to best possible. The bar at the top shows uncertainty from the selected range calculation. Monte Carlo shows variation across random samples; Best, Worst, High, Low, and Median collapse each answer range to one value.
results.contributions_var_size: This shows how much each answer contributed to each option. The green squares are good, while the red squares are bad. The size of the square is proportional to the weight of the factor. The percentages are essientially how "good" of an answer it is (compared to what we want it to be), and the numbers in the parenthesis are the given value/maximum value. This means that just like the previous graph, the area indicates the "usefulness" or "impactfulness", and the color indicates how good/bad that is compared to what we want it to be. These values are not relative to each other, but are on the objective scale that you set for each factor. The percentages are the percentage good it is (how close is the answer to what you want it be, on a scale of from the best it could be to the worst it could be)
results.factor_contributions: This graph shows how strongly each factor contributed to the selected option's result. Positive contributions extend above zero in green, while negative contributions extend below zero in red. The percentages won't add up to 100% because they are calculated as a percentage of the total distance from the optimal, not a percentage of the total contributions.

save.explanation: This page allows you to export and import decisions. You can export a decision as a .dec file, and import a .dec file.

explanation.explanation: This page explains the details of how the algorithm works. Let me know if I've explained it clearly enough, and if the graphs are helpful.

factor-packs.explanation:
If you're currently trying to make any of these decisions, these premade sets of factors might be helpful. These are just lists of things which relate to each decision which you might want to take into account, with units, mins/maxs, and optimal values pre-filled where applicable.

Note that these are just a starting point! You almost certainly have additional factors in your own life that apply to the decision. You can always add (or modify) factors later.

If none of these apply, you can move past this page.
